edits.before: Autonomous driving is the largest deployed autonomy system on Earth, and it got there before robot learning had a name. The distance between the two bookends is the whole story of this module. In 1988, ALVINN trained a three-layer neural network to steer a van from images from a camera and a laser range finder <Cite id="alvinn-1988" />. Its lineage went on to steer a van across America: in the 1995 No Hands Across America tour, the ALVINN-lineage RALPH program did the steering for 2,797 of 2,849 miles, 98.2 percent of the run, while the human researchers handled the throttle and brake <Cite id="no-hands-across-america-1995" />. In 2025, Waymo published a retrospective crash-rate study covering 56.7 million rider-only miles, miles driven with no human behind the steering wheel, and found statistically significant reductions against human benchmarks in every crash-outcome category it could statistically test <Cite id="waymo-crash-rates-2025" />. Between those bookends sits everything this wiki covers elsewhere: imitation learning, distribution shift, closed-loop evaluation, the long tail, and the gap between a working demo and a deployable system.
edits.after: Autonomous vehicles are cars and trucks that drive themselves, with sensors and software for perception, prediction, planning and control. The field runs from ALVINN, a 1988 neural network that steered a van from camera and laser range-finder images <Cite id="alvinn-1988" />, to Waymo robotaxis that gave more than 500,000 fully autonomous rides a week in April 2026 <Cite id="alphabet-q1-2026" />.

edits.before: For an ML engineer moving into robotics, AV is the field that already ran the experiment you are about to run. The sensor modalities differ, the action space is smaller, and the failure costs are higher, but the arguments are the same arguments: modular pipeline versus end-to-end learning, open-loop benchmarks versus closed-loop reality, and how much data it takes before the tail stops biting. This module covers the AV robotics stack, the reasons the problem remains open, and the specific lines along which AV work and robot learning continue to exchange methods.
edits.after: ALVINN trained on simulated road images <Cite id="alvinn-1988" />. By 1991 it learned to drive the Navlab van in under five minutes by watching a human driver <Cite id="pomerleau-1991" />. On the 1995 No Hands Across America tour, CMU's RALPH program steered for 2,797 of 2,849 miles, 98.2 percent, while the researchers handled throttle and brake <Cite id="no-hands-across-america-1995" />. Stanley won the 2005 DARPA Grand Challenge with software built mainly on machine learning and probabilistic reasoning <Cite id="stanley-2006" />.

edits.before: A production autonomous vehicle is built as a pipeline of distinct stages, each with its own models, its own metrics, and its own failure modes. The canonical decomposition is perception, prediction, planning, and control: what is around me, what will it do, what will I do about it, and how do I execute that decision through the car <Cite id="uniad-2023" />. The stages are standard enough that papers describe "modern autonomous driving systems" as "modular tasks in sequential order, i.e., perception, prediction, and planning" without further explanation <Cite id="uniad-2023" />. The table summarizes the division of labor; the sections after it fill in what each stage computes and where it breaks.
edits.after: A production autonomous vehicle is a pipeline of perception, prediction, planning and control, each with its own models, metrics and failure modes <Cite id="uniad-2023" /><Cite id="paden-2016" />. UniAD calls this "modular tasks in sequential order" <Cite id="uniad-2023" />. Paden's survey adds a vehicle-control layer below motion planning <Cite id="paden-2016" />.

edits.before: Perception turns raw sensor streams into a model of the scene: which objects exist, where they are, how they are moving, and what the road itself permits. The sensor suite is the first design decision, and it is the one that separates the industry's two camps. Waymo and most robotaxi operators fuse lidar, camera, and radar, paying for active range sensing that works in the dark and gives direct geometry. Camera-first programs bet that vision plus scale is enough and that lidar cost never amortizes. The public benchmark ecosystem grew up around the fused-sensor stack: the Waymo Open Dataset shipped 1,150 scenes of 20 seconds each, synchronized and calibrated lidar and camera data across urban and suburban geographies, and introduced a diversity metric under which it was 15 times more diverse than the largest existing camera-plus-lidar dataset <Cite id="waymo-open-dataset-2020" />.
edits.after:
Perception turns sensor streams into a model of the scene: which objects exist, where they are, how they move and what the road permits. Waymo's encoder fuses camera, lidar and radar inputs over time <Cite id="waymo-foundation-model-2025" />, and Waymo argues that no single sensor can replicate that redundant view <Cite id="waymo-ai-lessons-2026" />. BEVFormer, a camera-only bird's-eye-view detector, matched lidar-based baselines on the nuScenes test set <Cite id="bevformer-2022" />.

nuScenes, 1,000 scenes of 20 seconds, was the first dataset with a full vehicle sensor suite: 6 cameras, 5 radars and 1 lidar <Cite id="nuscenes-2020" />. The Waymo Open Dataset added 1,150 scenes of synchronized lidar and camera data <Cite id="waymo-open-dataset-2020" />. By its own metric it was 15 times more diverse than the largest earlier camera-plus-lidar set <Cite id="waymo-open-dataset-2020" />. Box detectors struggle with general, out-of-vocabulary objects, so the Occ3D benchmark predicts the occupancy and semantics of the whole scene <Cite id="occ3d-2023" />.

edits.before: Two representational ideas dominate perception research. The first is the bird's-eye view: project everything into a top-down grid aligned with the road, because downstream stages reason in that frame anyway. The second is occupancy, predicting which cells of that grid are occupied by anything at all, including object classes the detector was never trained on. Occupancy is the perception field's direct answer to the long tail: a mattress on the freeway does not need a class label to be something you should not drive into. Perception failures are the most expensive kind, because every later stage inherits them. The canonical case is Tempe, Arizona in March 2018, covered in detail below, where the system tracked a pedestrian for 5.6 seconds before impact while reclassifying her among three different categories, and never correctly predicted her path <Cite id="ntsb-uber-2019" />.
edits.after: Every later stage inherits a perception error. At Tempe in 2018 the system first detected a pedestrian 5.6 seconds before impact <Cite id="ntsb-uber-2019" />. It classified her in turn as a vehicle, an unknown object and a bicyclist, and never predicted her path correctly <Cite id="ntsb-uber-2019" />.

edits.before: Prediction, sometimes called behavior forecasting or motion prediction, estimates what every other agent in the scene will do over the next several seconds. It is the stage with no clean analogue in classical robotics and the one that made AV a machine learning problem rather than a controls problem. The central difficulty is that the future is multi-modal: at a four-way stop the crossing pedestrian may go or may wait, and a predictor that averages those futures produces a trajectory through both, which is a trajectory through neither.
edits.after: Prediction estimates what every other agent will do over the next several seconds. The future is multi-modal: a pedestrian may cross or wait, and a predictor that averages the two forecasts a path through neither. The Waymo Open Motion Dataset made interactive forecasting a benchmark: over 100,000 scenes of 20 seconds at 10 Hz, more than 570 hours over 1,750 km of roads <Cite id="waymo-open-motion-2021" />.

edits.before: The representational history of prediction is a story of replacing rendered rasters with structured input. Early systems drew agent histories and map features into a top-down image and ran a convolutional network over it. VectorNet replaced that with a hierarchical graph network operating directly on vectorized polylines, agent trajectories and HD-map entities as nodes with interactions between them, matching or beating the raster approach while saving over 70 percent of the model parameters and an order of magnitude in compute <Cite id="vectornet-2020" />. Vectorized representations became the default. Prediction quality is also where joint training started paying: systems that let the planner's needs shape the forecaster, rather than training the forecaster against its own metric, are the thread that leads directly to the unified architectures of 2023.
edits.after: Early predictors drew agent histories and map features into a top-down image for a convolutional network. VectorNet replaced that raster with a hierarchical graph network over vectorized polylines <Cite id="vectornet-2020" />. It matched or beat the raster with over 70 percent fewer parameters and an order of magnitude less computation <Cite id="vectornet-2020" />. MotionLM then cast multi-agent forecasting as language modeling over discrete motion tokens <Cite id="motionlm-2023" />.

edits.before: Planning decides what the ego vehicle will do: which route, which lane, what speed profile, and what trajectory through the next few seconds. The classical toolbox is deep here. The standard survey of the field organizes urban driving planning into route planning, behavior-level decision making (yield, overtake, merge), and local motion planning that respects vehicle dynamics, and the same survey covers the feedback-control layer that tracks the result <Cite id="paden-2016" />. Search, sampling, and trajectory optimization methods from that toolbox remain live production components; they are the same families covered in this wiki's classical modules on motion planning and control.
edits.after:
Planning decides the route, lane, speed profile and trajectory for the next few seconds. CMU's Boss won the 2007 DARPA Urban Challenge with a three-layer planner for mission, behavior and motion <Cite id="boss-urban-challenge-2008" />. Paden's survey splits urban planning the same way, with feedback control below <Cite id="paden-2016" />, the families covered under [motion planning](/classical/motion-planning/).

On nuPlan, the first closed-loop machine-learning planning benchmark <Cite id="nuplan-2021" />, an extremely simple planner built on rule-based priors won the 2023 challenge <Cite id="dauner-misconceptions-2023" />. Dauner and colleagues found learned planners limited in complex scenarios <Cite id="dauner-misconceptions-2023" />.

edits.before: The learned alternative arrived from imitation, and its history is a preview of robot learning's own. ChauffeurNet, Waymo's 2018 imitative planner, reported the finding that defines the field: standard behavior cloning over 30 million examples was not enough to drive robustly, even with a perception system preprocessing inputs and a controller executing outputs <Cite id="chauffeurnet-2018" />. The fix was to synthesize the worst: perturb the expert's trajectories into collisions and off-road excursions, and add losses that penalize those outcomes, so the learner sees recovery situations the log data never contains <Cite id="chauffeurnet-2018" />. That is the identical move robot manipulation would rediscover, and the reasons are the ones covered in Behavior Cloning Foundations: covariate shift means the states where you most need good actions are the states your logs underrepresent.
edits.after: ChauffeurNet, Waymo's 2018 imitative planner, found standard behavior cloning on 30 million examples insufficient, even with perception preparing its inputs and a controller executing its outputs <Cite id="chauffeurnet-2018" />. It perturbed the expert's driving into collisions and off-road excursions and added losses that penalize them <Cite id="chauffeurnet-2018" />. Manipulation later rediscovered that fix for covariate shift, as [behavior cloning foundations](/manipulation/bc-foundations/) explains.

edits.before:
Control is the layer that turns a planned trajectory into steering, brake, and throttle commands, and holds the vehicle on that trajectory despite disturbances, tire nonlinearity, and actuator delay. It is the oldest layer, the one with the strongest theory, and the one learning has displaced least. Lateral and longitudinal control loops, linear quadratic regulation, and model-predictive tracking, the families surveyed by Paden et al. and covered in this wiki's control module, remain the production standard <Cite id="paden-2016" />. A learned planner outputs a trajectory; a classical controller tracks it at high rate. The division is pragmatic: the controller runs at hundreds of hertz with provable stability margins, and nothing learned offers that contract.

Control is also where the vehicle's limits live. A trajectory that asks for more lateral acceleration than the tires can deliver is not trackable, and no amount of upstream intelligence fixes it. Planning systems therefore query a vehicle model before committing, and the whole stack treats the friction circle as a hard constraint. This is one structural difference from manipulation that will recur below: a car has no contact-rich manipulation phase, and its dynamics, while nonlinear, are well modeled, so the classical layer underneath the learning stays classical.
edits.after: Control turns a planned trajectory into steering, brake and throttle commands, and holds the vehicle on it despite disturbances, tire nonlinearity and actuator delay. Paden's survey covers the feedback path-tracking families: pure pursuit, Lyapunov-based trajectory tracking and model-predictive control <Cite id="paden-2016" />. A learned planner outputs a trajectory, and a classical [controller](/classical/control/) tracks it.

edits.before: The stack above describes the deployed industry default, but the research frontier has spent a decade pulling the stages together. The motivation is error propagation: each interface between stages is a lossy summary, and an error made upstream cannot be corrected downstream. The 2024 survey of end-to-end autonomous driving frames the trade precisely, noting that end-to-end systems benefit from joint feature optimization for perception and planning, at the cost of interpretability and the ability to debug a failed component in isolation <Cite id="e2e-ad-survey-2024" />.
edits.after: Each interface between stages is a lossy summary, and an upstream error cannot be corrected downstream. A 2024 survey frames the trade: end-to-end systems optimize perception and planning features jointly, while modular designs are easier to interpret and debug <Cite id="e2e-ad-survey-2024" />. UniAD kept the task structure but trained it as one network, with stages linked by unified query interfaces <Cite id="uniad-2023" />. Waymo's EMMA, built on a multimodal large language model foundation like Gemini, maps raw camera data to driving outputs written as text <Cite id="emma-2024" />.

edits.before: UniAD kept the task structure but trained the whole pipeline in one differentiable network, with perception, forecasting, and planning stages communicating through unified query interfaces, all oriented toward the planning objective rather than per-task metrics <Cite id="uniad-2023" />. It is a middle path: modular in structure, end-to-end in training. Waymo's EMMA went further, building on a multimodal large language model foundation in the Gemini family and representing all non-sensor inputs and outputs, navigation instructions, ego status, trajectories, 3D locations, as natural-language text, directly mapping camera input to driving outputs <Cite id="emma-2024" />. A driving policy that emits its plan as text is recognizably the same architectural bet as the vision-language-action models this wiki covers in its manipulation modules, and the comparison is drawn out below.
edits.after: On NAVSIM, open-loop results on real data did not reflect closed-loop performance <Cite id="navsim-2024" />. Simple methods such as TransFuser matched large architectures such as UniAD <Cite id="navsim-2024" />. Waymo says its own foundation model has significant benefits over both pure end-to-end and modular approaches <Cite id="waymo-foundation-model-2025" />.

edits.before: Three decades after ALVINN, robotaxis carry paying passengers in a handful of US cities, and the problem is still not solved. The honest statement of the situation has three parts: what "solved" would even mean, why the remaining distance is hard to close, and what the deployment record shows.
edits.after: Robotaxis now run at scale, and driving is still not solved. Waymo says it gave 15 million rides in 2025 and passed 20 million lifetime rides <Cite id="waymo-year-in-review-2025" />. By April 2026 it operated in 11 major US cities <Cite id="alphabet-q1-2026" />.

edits.before: The industry's own vocabulary concedes the point. SAE J3016, the standard taxonomy everyone uses, defines six levels of driving automation, 0 through 5, and its 2021 revision renamed levels 1 and 2 'Driver Support Systems' and sharpened the distinction between level 3 and level 4 <Cite id="sae-j3016-2021" />. Level 4 systems are deployed today, but every one of them operates inside an <Term id="operational-design-domain">operational design domain</Term>: a defined geography, road-type set, speed range, and weather envelope. Waymo's published safety comparisons are careful about this, aligning the human benchmark to the same vehicle types, road types, and locations the automated system operates in, so the comparison is not rigged <Cite id="waymo-crash-rates-2025" />. A system that drives Phoenix but not a Maine winter is a product with a boundary, not a solved problem, and expanding that boundary city by city remains manual, expensive engineering.
edits.after:
SAE J3016 defines six levels of driving automation, 0 through 5. Its 2021 revision named levels 1 and 2 "Driver Support Systems" and clarified the line between levels 3 and 4 <Cite id="sae-j3016-2021" />. Waymo calls improving a level 2 driver-assist system toward full autonomy "a false summit" <Cite id="waymo-ai-lessons-2026" />.

Every deployed level 4 system runs inside an <Term id="operational-design-domain">operational design domain</Term>, a defined geography, road set, speed range and weather envelope. Waymo's crash comparisons align the human benchmark to the same vehicle types, road types and locations <Cite id="waymo-crash-rates-2025" />.

On June 24, 2026, the UNECE World Forum for Harmonization of Vehicle Regulations adopted the first global regulations for fully autonomous driving systems <Cite id="un-ads-regulation-2026" />. Manufacturers must show that test environments, including virtual testing tools, meet strict credibility criteria, and that the system poses no unreasonable risk <Cite id="un-ads-regulation-2026" />. In the US, DOT and NHTSA announced an AV framework on April 24, 2025. On March 16, 2026, NHTSA proposed amending federal safety standards for automated vehicles without manual controls <Cite id="nhtsa-av-framework-2026" />.

In July 2026 NHTSA exempted Zoox's purpose-built robotaxi from parts of eight of those standards for commercial deployment <Cite id="nhtsa-zoox-exemption-2026" />. The exemption runs two years, for up to 2,500 vehicles in any 12-month period <Cite id="nhtsa-zoox-exemption-2026" />.

edits.before: The technical obstruction is the <Term id="long-tail">long tail</Term>: scenarios that are individually rare and collectively decisive. A mattress on the freeway at night, a traffic cop waving cars through a red light, a low sun behind a stopped fire truck. No natural driving log contains enough examples of any one of them to learn from, and the tail is unbounded, there is no finite list to check off. This is the same distribution-shift problem that pervades robot learning, concentrated by the safety requirement: an encounter you have never seen is exactly the encounter you are responsible for.
edits.after:
The technical obstruction is the <Term id="long-tail">long tail</Term>: scenarios that are individually rare and collectively decisive, such as an officer waving cars through a red light. No driving log holds enough of any one of them to learn from. Waymo's WOD-E2E benchmark collects 4,021 segments, about 12 hours, of scenarios that occur less than 0.03 percent of the time <Cite id="wod-e2e-2025" />.

Generative simulation is the industry's main answer. Waymo's World Model, built on Google DeepMind's Genie 3 and announced in February 2026, generates camera and lidar data controllable by driving actions, scene layout and language <Cite id="waymo-world-model-2026" />. Waymo built it to rehearse events "from a tornado to a casual encounter with an elephant" <Cite id="waymo-world-model-2026" />. The same post reported nearly 200 million fully autonomous miles on real roads and billions in virtual worlds <Cite id="waymo-world-model-2026" />.

Wayve's GAIA-2 likewise generates multi-camera driving video for common and rare scenarios <Cite id="gaia-2-2025" />. Whether such models cover the tail or only what their training data showed is open, as it is for [generative video](/world-models/generative-video/) in manipulation.

edits.before: The industry's main answer is simulation, and the current frontier of that answer is generative. Waymo's World Model, announced in February 2026 and built on Google DeepMind's Genie 3, generates camera and lidar simulation from real driving footage, controllable through driving actions, scene layout edits, and language prompts, and exists, in Waymo's own framing, to rehearse events "from a tornado to a casual encounter with an elephant" that are almost impossible to capture at scale in reality <Cite id="waymo-world-model-2026" />. The same post reports the scale of the flywheel: nearly 200 million fully autonomous miles on real roads, and billions of miles in virtual worlds <Cite id="waymo-world-model-2026" />. Whether a generative simulator covers the tail or only the parts of it its base model has seen is an open question, and it is the same question this wiki asks of generative world models for manipulation.
edits.after: The tail still produces recalls. In December 2025 Waymo recalled software on 3,067 vehicles that resumed driving past school buses with red lights flashing or stop arms extended <Cite id="waymo-recall-25e084-2025" />. In May 2026 it recalled 3,791 vehicles that could slow but not stop for an untraversable flooded lane on higher-speed roads <Cite id="waymo-recall-26e026-2026" />.

edits.before: Even a safe system has to prove it is safe, and the arithmetic of that proof is brutal. Kalra and Paddock's RAND study put numbers on it in 2016: demonstrating autonomous-vehicle reliability through test driving alone would take hundreds of millions of miles, and sometimes hundreds of billions, to provide clear statistical evidence of safety, because the crash rates being compared to are so low that real-world miles accumulate evidence glacially <Cite id="kalra-paddock-2016" />. Their conclusion was that on-road testing cannot be the primary safety case, a conclusion the industry internalized in its shift to simulation, scenario testing, and safety cases built on multiple evidence lines.
edits.after: Kalra and Paddock's 2016 RAND study found that test driving alone would need hundreds of millions of miles, sometimes hundreds of billions, to show safety <Cite id="kalra-paddock-2016" />. Mobileye's Responsibility-Sensitive Safety defines safe longitudinal and lateral distances as a white-box, interpretable model <Cite id="rss-2017" />. Its authors warned that without such standards the field risked a "winter of autonomous driving" <Cite id="rss-2017" />. Koopman argues that "safe enough" also requires no risk hot spots, such as reckless driving or risk shifted onto vulnerable populations, plus standards conformance and accountability <Cite id="koopman-safe-enough-2026" />.

edits.before: Formal approaches have been proposed to escape the statistics entirely. Mobileye's Responsibility-Sensitive Safety model specifies, as a white-box mathematical condition, what it means to drive safely in terms of safe distances in longitudinal and lateral motion, so that an attacker or auditor can check compliance without crash statistics <Cite id="rss-2017" />. Its authors were explicit that the goal was to make assurance verifiable and scalable, warning that without standardization the field risked a "winter of autonomous driving" <Cite id="rss-2017" />. The formal route has known limits: the model guarantees the vehicle behaved correctly by its own definition, which is not the same as never being in a crash, and learned perception does not expose the state estimates the formulas consume. Koopman's position is the complement: "safe enough" means more than crashes divided by miles, spanning net statistical safety, the absence of risk hot spots like reckless driving or shifted risk to vulnerable people, standards conformance, accountability, and meeting every stakeholder safety constraint, and treating safety as one number is how programs fool themselves <Cite id="koopman-safe-enough-2026" />.
edits.after: US companies must report crashes but not the miles they log, so crash rates are unknown for operators that do not volunteer mileage <Cite id="iihs-waymo-2026" />. NHTSA has also streamlined its Standing General Order on crash reporting <Cite id="nhtsa-av-framework-2026" />. California's DMV says its disengagement reports are not designed for comparison across companies, and deployment-permit operations need not report disengagements at all <Cite id="ca-dmv-av-miles-2026" />.

edits.before: The record itself cuts both ways, and both sides should be stated plainly. On one side: Waymo's 2025 study, covering 56.7 million rider-only miles through January 2025, found statistically significant lower crash rates than human benchmarks aligned to the same roads, across any-injury-reported, airbag-deployment, and suspected-serious-injury outcomes, with vehicle-to-vehicle intersection crashes reduced 96 percent in the any-injury category, and no statistically significant disbenefit in any of its eleven crash-type groups <Cite id="waymo-crash-rates-2025" />. That is a real, large, measured safety result, the first of its kind at that mileage.
edits.after:
Waymo's peer-reviewed 2025 study covered 56.7 million rider-only miles through January 2025 <Cite id="waymo-crash-rates-2025" />. Against human benchmarks on the same roads, it found statistically significant lower rates of any-injury-reported, airbag-deployment and suspected-serious-injury crashes <Cite id="waymo-crash-rates-2025" />. Vehicle-to-vehicle intersection crashes with any injury fell 96 percent, with no significant disbenefit in any of its 11 crash-type groups <Cite id="waymo-crash-rates-2025" />.

Waymo's own safety hub reports 271.3 million rider-only miles through June 2026 <Cite id="waymo-safety-hub-2026" />. Over the same distance it counts 95 percent fewer serious-injury-or-worse crashes and 82 percent fewer injury-causing crashes than human drivers <Cite id="waymo-safety-hub-2026" />. IIHS found that Waymo's driverless vehicles in San Francisco, Phoenix, Los Angeles and Austin had 68 percent fewer police-reportable crashes per mile than human drivers <Cite id="iihs-waymo-2026" />.

Tesla says it launched unsupervised rides in Miami, Orlando and Tampa in July 2026 and expanded its unsupervised area in Austin <Cite id="tesla-q2-2026-update" />. Baidu reported in August 2026 that Apollo Go had reached 28 cities and more than 240 million fully driverless kilometres <Cite id="baidu-q2-2026" />. Aurora began driverless customer deliveries between Dallas and Houston in May 2025 after closing its safety case <Cite id="aurora-driverless-launch-2025" />. By its count it drove nearly 440,000 driverless miles through June 2026 with zero collisions attributed to its system, and expected to end the year with 200 driverless trucks <Cite id="aurora-q2-2026" />.

On March 18, 2018, an Uber ATG test vehicle in Tempe, Arizona struck and killed a 49-year-old pedestrian crossing N. Mill Avenue at night, pushing a bicycle, where there was no crosswalk <Cite id="ntsb-uber-2019" />. The system judged a collision imminent 1.2 seconds before impact, and its design precluded emergency braking for crash mitigation alone, relying on the operator <Cite id="ntsb-uber-2019" />. The operator was streaming a television show, glancing down until about one second before the crash <Cite id="ntsb-uber-2019" />. Every layer failed at once, the correlated-safeguard problem the [reliability gap](/frontier/reliability-gap/) article examines.

edits.before: On the other side: the road there included the field's defining failure. On March 18, 2018, an Uber ATG test vehicle in Tempe, Arizona struck and killed a pedestrian, Elaine Herzberg, crossing N. Mill Avenue at night, pushing a bicycle, where there was no crosswalk <Cite id="ntsb-uber-2019" />. The NTSB's findings read as a checklist of everything this module has described. Perception detected her 5.6 seconds before impact but reclassified her among vehicle, unknown object, and bicycle, never correctly predicting her path <Cite id="ntsb-uber-2019" />. The system determined a collision was imminent 1.2 seconds before impact, by then outside its braking response specification, and its design precluded emergency braking for collision mitigation, relying on the operator instead <Cite id="ntsb-uber-2019" />. The operator, who was supposed to be the redundant safeguard, was streaming a television show on her phone, glancing down for extended periods until about one second before the crash <Cite id="ntsb-uber-2019" />. A classification failure, propagated through a planning stack that could not brake, "protected" by a human who was not watching: every layer failed at once. The lesson generalizes past AV, and it is the reliability argument this wiki makes elsewhere in depth: a chain of human-in-the-loop safeguards is not a safety case, because the safeguards correlate exactly when they matter.
edits.after: On October 2, 2023, a driverless Cruise vehicle dragged a pedestrian about 20 feet before stopping. Under a September 2024 consent order, Cruise agreed to a \$1.5 million penalty for crash reports that omitted those details <Cite id="nhtsa-cruise-consent-2024" />. In December 2024 GM stopped funding Cruise's robotaxi work, citing the time and resources needed to scale it <Cite id="gm-cruise-refocus-2024" />.

edits.before: The two fields are branches of one lineage. The imitation learning toolkit was built on driving before it was applied to arms. ALVINN was behavior cloning in 1988 <Cite id="alvinn-1988" />. DAgger, the canonical fix for covariate shift, was motivated substantially by the driving setting, and its quadratic-to-linear regret improvement is stated over exactly the horizon compounding that long driving tasks exhibit <Cite id="dagger-2011" />. ChauffeurNet's discovery that 30 million demonstrations do not save naive cloning, and its move of synthesizing worst-case perturbations, predates and predicts everything in this wiki's module on behavior cloning foundations <Cite id="chauffeurnet-2018" />. When an embodied-AI engineer today argues about action chunking versus per-step prediction, the argument is a descendant of arguments AV researchers had about trajectory horizon a decade ago.
edits.after:
The imitation toolkit was built on driving before it reached arms. DAgger, the canonical fix for covariate shift, was demonstrated on steering a car in a 3D racing game <Cite id="dagger-2011" />. It cuts the growth of mistakes over the horizon from quadratic to linear <Cite id="dagger-2011" />. On 500,000 hours of driving, Waymo found that forecasting and planning improve as a power law in compute, and closed-loop metrics improve too <Cite id="waymo-scaling-laws-2025" />.

RAD trains end-to-end policies by reinforcement learning in photorealistic 3D Gaussian splatting replicas, to address imitation's causal confusion and open-loop gap <Cite id="rad-2025" />. It reports a 3x lower collision rate <Cite id="rad-2025" />.

edits.before: The current architectural convergence is not an analogy, it is the same architecture. EMMA is a vision-language model with driving outputs represented as text, jointly trained across planning, detection, and road-graph tasks, and evaluated as a generalist <Cite id="emma-2024" />. That is a <Term id="vision-language-action-model">vision-language-action model</Term> whose embodiment is a car. The survey literature now treats it as such: a late-2025 survey of VLA models for autonomous driving maps the field into end-to-end VLA, one model from sensors to actions, and dual-system VLA, a slow deliberative VLM over a fast safety-critical executor <Cite id="vla-ad-survey-2026" />. Read that taxonomy against this wiki's manipulation modules and it is the same fault line: end-to-end VLA versus hierarchical system, π0 versus SayCan descendants, with the same open question of where the safety-critical fast path should live. The dual-system framing in driving is argued on exactly the grounds manipulation uses for knowledge insulation and real-time execution: a large model's inference budget does not close a 10 Hz control loop.
edits.after:
EMMA is a vision-language model co-trained as a generalist on planning, detection and road-graph tasks, with its driving outputs written as text <Cite id="emma-2024" />. It is a <Term id="vision-language-action-model">vision-language-action model</Term> whose embodiment is a car. A late-2025 survey splits driving VLAs into end-to-end models, which perceive, reason and plan in one network, and dual-system models, where a slow VLM deliberates over fast, safety-critical execution <Cite id="vla-ad-survey-2026" />.

Waymo's foundation model uses such a "Think Fast and Think Slow" design, a sensor-fusion encoder for rapid reactions beside a driving VLM trained using Gemini <Cite id="waymo-foundation-model-2025" />. The split mirrors the end-to-end versus [hierarchical](/manipulation/hierarchical/) divide in manipulation and the [knowledge insulation](/manipulation/knowledge-insulation/) case for a separate fast path. NVIDIA reports that its Alpamayo-R1 driving VLA runs on the vehicle in real time at 99 ms latency <Cite id="alpamayo-r1-2025" />.

edits.before: Data practice is converging the same way. The Waymo Open Dataset's 1,150 scenes set the pattern AV research still follows: shared perception benchmarks with defined metrics <Cite id="waymo-open-dataset-2020" />. Robot learning's Open X-Embodiment pool, over a million trajectories across 22 embodiments federated from dozens of labs, is the same bet on shared data as the substrate for generalist policies <Cite id="open-x-embodiment-2023" />. The scales differ in kind, tens of hours versus millions of miles of driving logs, which is the subject of this wiki's data bottleneck module, but the strategic move, pool heterogeneous real data, standardize the format, train generalists, is identical.

edits.before: Three structural differences keep the fields from merging outright, and they are worth internalizing because they explain why results transfer unevenly.
edits.after: A car steers and accelerates through two channels governed by tire friction and well-studied vehicle models. A manipulator moves dozens of joints that make and break contact. The <Term id="mpc">model-predictive control</Term> that tracks a car's trajectory <Cite id="paden-2016" /> has no equally clean purchase on a robot wiping a table, the argument of [why RL won locomotion](/rl-sim2real/why-rl-locomotion/).

edits.before: First, the action space and its dynamics. A car's decision variables are steering angle and longitudinal acceleration, two channels, governed by tire friction and a century of vehicle modeling. Manipulation's action space is dozens of joints making and breaking contact with objects whose physics are discontinuous at the contact boundary. The <Term id="mpc">model-predictive control</Term> that still runs a car's tracking layer has no equally clean purchase on a robot wiping a table, which is the subject of this wiki's module on why RL won locomotion but not manipulation: simulability of the transition function, not intelligence, is what separates the domains <Cite id="paden-2016" />.
edits.after: Evaluation differs too. Waymo says replaying recorded data in open-loop simulation is insufficient <Cite id="waymo-ai-lessons-2026" />, and nuPlan moved planning evaluation from open-loop L2 metrics to closed-loop simulation <Cite id="nuplan-2021" />. Manipulation still reports short-horizon success on small trial counts, the subject of the [evaluation crisis](/data-hardware/evaluation-crisis/).

edits.before:
Second, evaluation. AV evaluation is closed-loop and statistical by necessity, crash rates over hundreds of millions of miles, benchmark simulators, and now regulatory reporting. Manipulation evaluation is still dominated by open-loop or short-horizon task success on small trial counts, the subject of this wiki's evaluation crisis module. The transfer direction is clear, and it is from AV to robotics: the discipline of reporting miles, interventions, and statistical confidence is what robot learning needs as its policies reach deployment.

Third, the simulator question. AV simulation got good enough to be load-bearing because driving is, in the end, rigid-body kinematics plus appearance, with no contact-rich manipulation phase. The Waymo World Model generating camera and lidar for edge-case rehearsal is the strongest deployed argument anywhere that generative world models can carry a safety case <Cite id="waymo-world-model-2026" />. Robot learning is attempting the same move with Genie-class models whose action-conditioning is still weak, the central open problem this wiki's generative video module documents <Cite id="genie-3-2025" />. Driving is the easy case of world modeling, low-dimensional actions and no contact, and the fact that it took a Genie 3 derivative to make it work at scale is the calibrator for how far manipulation still has to go.
edits.after: Driving simulation covers rigid-body motion and appearance with no contact-rich phase, and Waymo says its World Model helps it scale its service safely <Cite id="waymo-world-model-2026" />. Robot learning attempts the same with Genie-class models whose range of actions is still constrained <Cite id="genie-3-2025" />.

edits.before: The two fields will keep trading. The items most likely to matter to a robotics engineer: whether dual-system VLA architectures in driving stabilize into the same shape as hierarchical manipulation systems, which would validate the insulation recipe across embodiments <Cite id="vla-ad-survey-2026" />; whether generative simulators expand beyond appearance into contact, where manipulation lives; and whether the safety-case machinery AV built under regulatory pressure, formal models like RSS, statistical deployment studies, and audit standards <Cite id="rss-2017" />, gets imported into robotics before robots deploy at scale, rather than after. The reliability gap module carries that argument forward for manipulation specifically, and the [drones module](/adjacent/drones) shows the same simulability argument already settled at higher bandwidth in the air.
edits.after: One open question is whether dual-system driving VLAs settle into the shape of hierarchical manipulation systems <Cite id="vla-ad-survey-2026" />. edits.before: Drones are aircraft that fly with no pilot on board. A quadrotor is among the most agile machines ever built, and it is the robot that learned to control itself first. Racing quadrotors pull forces several times their own weight, exceed 100 km/h, and accelerate at several times gravity in confined spaces <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" />. The same airframe costs a few hundred dollars, carries its own sensors and compute, and crashes without breaking anything but itself. That combination, extreme dynamics plus cheap iteration, is why autonomous flight went from a controls problem to a learning problem a full decade before manipulation did, and why the results came faster: by 2021 a neural network flew a drone through forests, outperforming classical obstacle-avoidance pipelines <Cite id="high-speed-flight-2021" />, and by 2023 a reinforcement-learning system beat three human world champions at their own sport <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" />.
edits.after: Aerial robotics is the design and control of robots that fly, from delivery drones and racing quadrotors to <Term id="swarm-robotics">swarms</Term>. Flight was an early learning success because its dynamics simulate well: a reinforcement-learning system beat human world champions in its own lab in 2023 <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" />, and a one-camera drone won an organiser-run race in 2025 <Cite id="monorace-2026" />.

edits.before:
This module covers the two halves of aerial robotics that matter to an ML engineer moving into robotics: autonomous flight, where the field's sim-to-real and learning-versus-control arguments were settled first, and <Term id="swarm-robotics">swarm robotics</Term>, where many cheap flying robots coordinate through local interaction. The treatment is honest about scope: these are domains where the core problems are closer to solved than manipulation is, and the reasons trace back to one structural fact about the dynamics.

The hardest constraint on a flying robot is below, and it is not the control law. Switch the drone below between an ordinary camera, which takes about 70 ms to report what it sees, and a faster event camera, and try each swerve setting: the top safe speed moves with every choice. No controller recovers what latency has already spent.

edits.before: The comparison this wiki keeps returning to is simulability: reinforcement learning wins wherever the transition function is cheap to simulate, and loses where it is not. A quadrotor is the benign case twice over. Its dynamics are differentially flat, meaning the full state follows from a small set of outputs, and a century of aerodynamics gives accurate thrust and drag models. There is no contact: an aerial robot either flies in free space or it has already failed. Sim-to-real for flight therefore needs domain randomization over motor constants and sensor noise, while manipulation also contends with friction and deformation, which is the wall the manipulation literature keeps hitting.
edits.after:
A quadrotor is a benign case for simulation. Its dynamics are differentially flat in position and heading, even with linear rotor drag <Cite id="faessler-flatness-2018" />, and standard models cover its dynamics, estimation and control <Cite id="mahony-multirotor-2012" />. Flight also has no contact: an aerial robot either flies in free space or has already failed. Racing quadrotors still exceed 100 km/h and accelerate at several times gravity <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" />.

Classical stacks plan a trajectory and then track it. Mellinger and Kumar generated minimum-snap trajectories for quadrotors <Cite id="mellinger-minimum-snap-2011" />, and Lee and colleagues built a geometric tracking controller on SE(3) <Cite id="lee-se3-control-2010" />. In 2021 time-optimal trajectory planning outperformed professional human pilots in racing <Cite id="foehn-time-optimal-2021" />.

Swift, from the University of Zurich, raced three human champions, including the world champions of two leagues, and won several races against each <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" />. It trained its control policy in simulation with model-free reinforcement learning <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" />. The team then fitted residual models of perception noise and unmodeled dynamics from real flight data and retrained <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" />.

In September 2023, Song and colleagues showed that an RL controller outperformed optimal control on the same racing task <Cite id="racing-rl-vs-oc-2023" />. Optimal control splits the problem into planning and control with a trajectory as the interface, which limits the controller under unmodeled effects. RL optimizes a task-level objective directly and handles model uncertainty through domain randomization; it flew above 12 g and 108 km/h <Cite id="racing-rl-vs-oc-2023" />. A later hybrid embedded a differentiable MPC in an actor-critic framework and matched model-free RL at up to 21 m/s <Cite id="ac-mpc-2026" />.

edits.before: The empirical result that made this concrete came from the racing track. Swift, the University of Zurich system that beat drone-racing champions in 2023, trained its control policy entirely in simulation with model-free reinforcement learning <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" />. The gap to the physical world was closed by measuring the gap: the team recorded real flight data, fitted residual models of perception noise and unmodeled dynamics, injected them into the simulator, and retrained <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" />. The same recipe, empirical residual modeling on top of a clean simulator, is what legged locomotion uses and what manipulation still struggles to copy because its residuals are the whole problem.
edits.after: In April 2025 a TU Delft drone with one rolling-shutter camera and an IMU won the A2RL race in Abu Dhabi, beating all AI teams and three human world champions in a knockout tournament <Cite id="monorace-2026" />. TU Delft notes that Swift raced in a lab where the researchers controlled conditions, hardware and track, while the A2RL organisers designed both hardware and track <Cite id="tudelft-a2rl-2025" />.

edits.before: A year later the same group published the controlled comparison the debate needed. Song and colleagues raced an optimal-control stack against a reinforcement-learning policy on the same platform, method by method, and found the RL controller faster <Cite id="racing-rl-vs-oc-2023" />. Their diagnosis matters more than the result: RL's advantage came from its task-level objective, which removed the planner-to-tracker interface. Optimal control decomposes the problem into trajectory planning plus tracking, and the planned trajectory becomes an interface that limits what the controller can express when reality disagrees with the model; RL optimizes the task-level reward directly and absorbs model error through domain randomization <Cite id="racing-rl-vs-oc-2023" />. The flown result was a peak acceleration above 12 times gravity and a peak velocity of 108 km/h <Cite id="racing-rl-vs-oc-2023" />. Read that against this wiki's module on why RL won locomotion but not manipulation: flight is locomotion's argument at higher bandwidth, with the same moral.
edits.after: In January 2026 world FPV champion Minchan Kim beat TII Racing's drone from a 4 to 4 tie when it struck a gate and could not recover <Cite id="a2rl-2026-final" />. Champion policies stay narrow: they often crash immediately in unseen configurations, and a 2026 method improved generalization 7.4x <Cite id="green-generalization-2026" />.

edits.before: An autonomous drone runs the same stages an autonomous car does, compressed by three orders of magnitude in size and power. Perception is a camera plus an inertial measurement unit; state estimation is <Term id="visual-inertial-odometry">visual-inertial odometry</Term>, fusing image features against IMU accelerations to produce the metric pose and velocity the controller needs, with no GPS and no external motion capture <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" />. Planning is a local trajectory toward the goal; control tracks it at hundreds of hertz. The stages interact exactly as the driving stack does, and one of them, the perception latency, sets a hard ceiling on everything downstream.
edits.after: One camera and one low-cost IMU are the minimum sensor suite for metric six-DoF state estimation <Cite id="vins-mono-2018" />. <Term id="visual-inertial-odometry">Visual-inertial odometry</Term> fuses image features with IMU measurements into the pose and velocity the controller needs, without GPS or motion capture <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" />. The fast inner loop often runs on a microcontroller stack such as PX4, which has substantially lower latency than a typical robotics Linux system <Cite id="px4-2015" />.

edits.before: The latency argument is the cleanest result in aerial robotics, and the figure at the top of this module reproduces it. Falanga, Kim, and Scaramuzza asked a direct question: how fast can a drone fly, given the latency of its perception pipeline and the acceleration its airframe can produce <Cite id="falanga-latency-2019" />? Their answer is a closed-form inequality. A drone flying at speed v perceives an obstacle when it enters the sensing range s, but the perception pipeline delays the information by the latency tau. The time to contact left when control finally acts is s/v minus tau, and the avoidance maneuver at maximum lateral acceleration u takes time proportional to the square root of the obstacle size over u. If the remaining time is shorter than the maneuver, no controller saves the drone: the crash is set by geometry before any control law runs. The maximum speed follows directly, range divided by latency plus maneuver time <Cite id="falanga-latency-2019" />.
edits.after:
Falanga, Kim and Scaramuzza asked how fast a drone can fly given its perception latency and the acceleration its airframe can produce <Cite id="falanga-latency-2019" />. A drone at speed $v$ sees an obstacle at sensing range $s$, and its pipeline delays that information by latency $\tau$. Avoiding the obstacle at maximum lateral acceleration $u$ takes time proportional to the square root of obstacle size over $u$. If $s/v - \tau$ is shorter than the maneuver, no controller saves the drone <Cite id="falanga-latency-2019" />.

A 70 ms stereo pipeline, the upper bound the study took from a commercial camera's datasheet, supports about 19 m/s at 25 m/s² of lateral acceleration and 25 m/s at 50 m/s² <Cite id="falanga-latency-2019" />. An event camera reports per-pixel brightness changes without waiting for a frame. At 8 m of range its ceiling is 7 percent higher on the least agile airframe and 22 percent higher at 50 m/s², 31.03 against 25.40 m/s. The paper's own summary of 7 to 12 percent is for its most agile airframe, at 200 m/s², against the fastest stereo camera <Cite id="falanga-latency-2019" />.

edits.before: The numbers make the argument sharp. A stereo camera pipeline with a 70 ms latency, the upper bound the study took from a commercial stereo camera's datasheet, supports about 19 m/s on an airframe that can pull 25 m/s^2 laterally, and 25 m/s on one that can pull 50 <Cite id="falanga-latency-2019" />. The paper's comparison point is the event camera, a sensor that reports per-pixel brightness changes without waiting out a frame; at 8 m of sensing range its ceiling runs 7 percent above the stereo one on the study's least agile airframe and 22 percent at 50 m/s^2, 31.03 versus 25.40 m/s in its table, and the paper's own summary of 7 to 12 percent spans the least agile airframe across sensing ranges <Cite id="falanga-latency-2019" />. The structural lesson generalizes past sensors: latency anywhere in the loop, sensing, inference, or actuation, converts directly into a speed ceiling or a crash margin, and faster platforms tolerate less of it. A vision-language-action model that takes 50 ms to infer one action is slow on any robot. On a fast drone it is also the binding constraint on the whole system.
edits.after: In 2020 an event-camera quadrotor dodged fast-moving objects using only onboard sensing and computation <Cite id="falanga-event-avoidance-2020" />. Vision-language-action flight is far slower: RaceVLA averaged 1.04 m/s with a top speed of 2.02 m/s <Cite id="racevla-2025" />. On the CognitiveDrone benchmark RaceVLA succeeded 31.3 percent of the time, and CognitiveDrone-R1, which adds a reasoning module, 77.2 percent <Cite id="cognitivedrone-2025" />.

edits.before: The modular stack's weakness on a drone is the same one the driving literature found: each interface between stages is a lossy summary, and latency accumulates across the pipeline. The aerial answer arrived in 2021. Loquercio and colleagues trained a convolutional network to map noisy depth images directly to collision-free trajectories, in a receding-horizon loop, trained entirely in simulation by imitating an expert with privileged information <Cite id="high-speed-flight-2021" />. The key transfer trick was realistic sensor noise in training: simulate the noise properties of the real depth sensor and the policy stops overfitting to clean inputs, and it crossed from simulation to real forests, snow, derailed trains, and collapsed buildings with zero additional training on them <Cite id="high-speed-flight-2021" />. Their own framing of the result is the pipeline critique stated plainly: separating sensing, mapping, and planning "can be problematic for high-speed navigation in cluttered environments" because the stages run sequentially, latency compounds, and errors propagate <Cite id="high-speed-flight-2021" />.
edits.after:
Deep Drone Acrobatics trained a policy entirely in simulation by imitating an optimal controller with privileged information, and flew maneuvers at up to 3 g <Cite id="deep-drone-acrobatics-2020" />. In 2021 Loquercio and colleagues used the same recipe to map noisy depth images directly to collision-free trajectories <Cite id="high-speed-flight-2021" />. With realistic simulated sensor noise, the policy transferred to forests, snow, derailed trains and collapsed buildings with no additional training. The authors argue that separating sensing, mapping and planning "can be problematic for high-speed navigation in cluttered environments" because latency compounds and errors propagate <Cite id="high-speed-flight-2021" />.

Swift kept a modular front end: a visual-inertial estimator and a gate-detection network feed a Kalman filter, and a small two-layer RL network maps that state to collective thrust and body rates <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" />. Later systems drop explicit state estimation. Geles and colleagues fly from pixels with the thrust and body-rate commands human pilots use <Cite id="geles-pixels-2024" />, and Dream to Fly learned racing from pixels with a world model where PPO and SAC struggled <Cite id="dream-to-fly-2025" />.

edits.before: Swift sits in the middle of the same spectrum. Swift uses multiple components: a visual-inertial estimator plus a gate-detection network produce a low-dimensional state estimate, a Kalman filter fuses them, and a small two-layer network trained by reinforcement learning maps that state to collective thrust and body rates <Cite id="swift-drone-racing-2023" />. The learned part is the control, the classical parts are estimation, and the split follows the latency argument: perception can afford to be a pipeline because its output is a state vector, while control must be learned to exploit the platform's limits. That division, classical estimation under learned control, is the closest thing aerial robotics has to a consensus architecture, and it is the same shape the manipulation field arrived at from the other direction with real-time chunking over a learned policy.

edits.before: The second half of aerial robotics multiplies the robots. A swarm is many cheap platforms coordinating to do what one expensive platform cannot: cover a search area, map a forest, or fly a light show. The field's founding models came from biology, Reynolds' 1987 flocking model being the canonical one <Cite id="reynolds-boids-1987" />, and treat the group as a dynamical system of local attraction and repulsion terms. Those models explain collective motion, and they have been flown: Vásárhelyi and colleagues optimized the interaction terms and flew 30 drones in coherent outdoor flocking <Cite id="vasarhelyi-flocking-2018" />. What they do not provide is guarantees, because reactive potential fields have no lookahead, get trapped in local minima, and have no notion of the platform's dynamics.

Space robotics is the domain where the two assumptions of everyday robotics fail at once. There is no repair: a rover on Mars cannot be serviced, and a satellite that fails in geosynchronous orbit is written off or, at best, visited once by a purpose-built spacecraft. And there is no live supervision: a signal between Earth and Mars takes minutes to arrive and minutes to return, so no operator closes a control loop in real time. Everything this wiki's manipulation modules treat as hard, generalization and dexterity, is secondary in space; everything they treat as background, reliability and verification, is the entire engineering problem. The result is a field that runs decades behind terrestrial robotics in raw capability and decades ahead of it in discipline, and both facts trace back to the same constraint.

This module covers the three places that discipline is visible. First the NASA/JPL rover program, which is the longest-running deployment of field autonomy anywhere, and the only one where autonomy is forced by physics, irrespective of capability. Second <Term id="in-situ-resource-utilization">in-situ resource utilization</Term>, or ISRU, the program of turning local material into propellant and consumables, whose robotics half is excavation and drilling under the worst conditions manipulation has. Third <Term id="on-orbit-servicing">on-orbit servicing</Term>: rendezvous, capture, refueling, and debris removal, the one branch of space robotics that has become a commercial industry in the last five years.

## Autonomy paced by the speed of light

A Mars rover operates on a cadence set by physics. The operations team plans a sol's activity during the previous sol, uplinks the sequence in a single communication window, and receives the results after the rover has already executed them. Under that cadence, every second of onboard decision-making is worth trading against bandwidth. NASA/JPL's autonomy program optimizes for that constraint; its progress cannot be judged on capability alone.

The numbers from Perseverance, published by its own autonomy team, show how far that optimization has gone. In the rover's first Mars year, its AutoNav system evaluated 88 percent of the 17.7 kilometers the vehicle traveled, and the previous record for autonomous distance evaluation was 2.4 kilometers, accumulated by Opportunity over fourteen years <Cite id="perseverance-autonomy-2023" />. AutoNav has driven 699.9 meters without a human reviewing the imagery, and 347.7 meters in a single sol, both planetary rover records <Cite id="perseverance-autonomy-2023" />. None of this is learned control in the sense of this wiki's policy modules; it is stereo vision, terrain assessment, and trajectory evaluation, engineered and verified a decade before flight. The one place a classifier sits inside the loop is targeting: the AEGIS system analyzes wide-angle imagery onboard and autonomously selects targets for the SuperCam instrument, so scientifically interesting targets get observed during or immediately after long drives without waiting for a ground communication cycle <Cite id="perseverance-autonomy-2023" />. AEGIS was first deployed on Curiosity in 2016, where onboard target selection for the ChemCam laser spectrometer measurably increased science data return <Cite id="aegis-curiosity-2017" />. That is the honest picture of learning in deep space: a bounded decision, inside a classical system, adopted because it spends bandwidth better than a human in the loop.

The same culture of designing for the case that cannot be retrieved explains the Ingenuity helicopter. On April 19, 2021, Ingenuity became the first aircraft to make a powered, controlled flight on another planet <Cite id="ingenuity-first-flight-2021" />, in an atmosphere with about one percent of Earth's surface pressure, which is the reason nothing about the flight could be tested as-flown before launch. It was qualified as a technology demonstration: five flights over thirty days. It flew 72 times over almost three years before NASA concluded the mission in January 2024 <Cite id="ingenuity-mission-end-2024" />. A fourteen-fold margin over the design life is what verification-heavy engineering buys when the design point itself is conservative, and it is the same relationship between claim and evidence this wiki keeps asking of manipulation results, running in the opposite direction.

## Living off the land: ISRU

ISRU is the engineering name for living off the land: producing mission consumables at the destination instead of launching them. The propellant needed to lift a crew off Mars and send it home would dominate an all-Earth-supplied mass budget, which is why the first demonstration of the technology on another planet was an oxygen generator. MOXIE, riding on Perseverance, electrolyzed carbon dioxide from the Martian atmosphere in a solid-oxide cell; across sixteen runs it produced 122 grams of oxygen, peaking at 12 grams per hour at 98 percent purity or better, about twice NASA's original production goals, before concluding operations in September 2023 <Cite id="moxie-completion-2023" />.

MOXIE is an instrument, and instruments do not shovel. Scaled ISRU is a robotics problem: drilling, excavating, and moving granular material in vacuum, at cryogenic temperatures, with abrasive dust, over maintenance-free years. The first American attempt to exercise that hardware on the Moon is a case study in how partial the data comes back. NASA's PRIME-1 suite flew to the lunar south pole on Intuitive Machines' IM-2 lander in March 2025. The lander, Athena, came to rest on its side in a crater about 400 meters from its target site, and the mission ran roughly ten hours against the ten days planned <Cite id="prime-1-lunar-2025" />. Within that window the hardware itself worked: TRIDENT, a one-metre rotary-percussive drill built by Honeybee Robotics, executed its commanded motions into the regolith, and the MSOLO mass spectrometer ran its scans, though the gases it detected were all of human origin, propellant and traces of Earth water, with no lunar volatiles detected <Cite id="prime-1-lunar-2025" />. NASA's own summary is precise about what was and was not demonstrated, and it is worth reading as the ISRU program's real progress bar: the mechanisms survived the environment and obeyed commands, while the science return was lost to a landing accident upstream of them <Cite id="prime-1-lunar-2025" />. Compare that with the evaluation-crisis module's argument about bench results: in space, the environment gets a vote on every trial, and the first trial of a new capability is often also the last one available for years.

Learned locomotion meets the same regolith in analogue tests on the ground. In October 2026, Adrian Fuhrer, Marco Hutter and colleagues at ETH Zurich reported on a 2025 campaign in the ESA/DLR LUNA lunar analogue facility in Cologne, where the quadrupeds ANYmal-D and Magnecko walked loose regolith simulant and crater-like terrain. The robots could cross the simulant, but sinkage and slip, dust kicked up by foot contacts, and perception failures from overexposure, shadows and low-texture ground all degraded performance <Cite id="luna-legged-2026" />.

## Orbital robotics: servicing and removal

The second tradition of space robotics operates closer to home, where the machines can at least be reached. On-orbit servicing is a rendezvous and manipulation problem: arrive at a target moving kilometers per second, match its motion to centimeters per second, then either dock with hardware that was never designed to be docked with or grasp hardware that was never designed to be grasped.

<OrbitalServicingTable className="my-6 wide-measure" />

The table reads as one lineage. Japan's ETS-VII demonstrated autonomous rendezvous and docking between two spacecraft in 1998, along with the flight experiments for a two-metre, six-degree-of-freedom manipulator mounted on one of them <Cite id="ets-vii-ard-2001" /><Cite id="ets-vii-robot-2001" />. DARPA's Orbital Express put the full servicing sequence together in 2007: over a four-month flight demonstration, the ASTRO servicer autonomously captured its NextSat client, transferred propellant to it, and robotically exchanged a battery with it <Cite id="orbital-express-2008" />. The International Space Station runs the operational version of the same machinery every week: Canadarm2, a 17-metre arm that assembled the station and still performs the cosmic catches, grappling arriving cargo vehicles and berthing them <Cite id="canadarm2-csa-2024" />, while Dextre, a two-armed robot riding the same arm, replaces exterior equipment including the station's 100-kilogram batteries, all of it <Term id="teleoperation">teleoperation</Term> planned and flown by a ground crew <Cite id="dextre-csa-2024" />. What the station proves, at twenty-plus years of continuous operation, is that durable space manipulation is possible when the machine is maintained, reachable, and supervised, which is exactly what a satellite in a graveyard orbit is not.

The commercial era started in 2020, when Northrop Grumman's MEV-1 performed the first docking between two commercial spacecraft in orbit, capturing the Intelsat 901 broadcast satellite in the graveyard orbit above geosynchronous altitude and returning it to service <Cite id="mev1-servicing-2025" />. Five years later, with the client's life extension complete, MEV-1 undocked, the first undocking between commercial spacecraft in that orbit, and moved on to its next servicing mission <Cite id="mev1-servicing-2025" />. Life extension by docking is deliberately conservative robotics: the client satellite is cooperative, three-axis stabilized, and expects the visit. The frontier case is the client that cooperates with nobody. Astroscale's ADRAS-J, flying for JAXA's debris-removal program, rendezvoused with a discarded rocket upper stage during 2024, inspected it with three fly-around surveys, and on its final approach closed to about 15 metres, the closest any commercial spacecraft has come to a piece of debris through rendezvous and proximity operations <Cite id="adras-j-15m-2024" />. That approach ended in an autonomous abort, the onboard collision-avoidance system reacting to an unexpected attitude anomaly on the dead stage, which is the demonstration working as designed: the hard part of debris removal is the trust required to close the last 15 metres at all <Cite id="adras-j-15m-2024" />.

The honest counterweight to this progress is NASA's own OSAM-1, a mission meant to demonstrate refueling a satellite that had not been prepared for service. In March 2024, after an independent review, NASA discontinued the project, citing continued technical, cost, and schedule challenges and a broader community shift away from refueling unprepared spacecraft, with no committed partner remaining <Cite id="osam1-discontinued-2024" />. A flagship servicing demonstration dying of cost growth, in the same decade the commercial servicers began operating, is not a contradiction. It is the economics of the reliability bar: servicing pays when the client is expensive and the servicer is reusable, and every unserviced design that launches resets the market backward.

## What robot learning takes from it

Three transfers, none of them about hardware.

First, the latency argument from the drones module, completed at solar-system scale. The perception-latency study cited there measures how milliseconds of pipeline delay cap a drone's safe speed; light-time delay is the same mechanism with the constant set by physics instead of engineering, and its product is an unsupervised robot <Cite id="perseverance-autonomy-2023" />. Any robot whose control loop cannot close through a human, a Mars rover during a drive, a servicing spacecraft in final approach, must either freeze its policy before deployment or carry the whole decision onboard. That is the deep reason space autonomy is classical: a verified stereo pipeline can be argued about line by line before launch, and a policy trained on ten thousand demonstrations cannot, yet.

Second, the reliability bar, which this domain shares with the [surgical robotics](/adjacent/surgical) module and pushes further. The surgical field deploys at Level 0 autonomy because each increment must be individually cleared; space robotics deploys bounded autonomy only after test-like-you-fly verification, and its failures are instructive in both directions: Ingenuity exceeded its qualification fourteen-fold <Cite id="ingenuity-mission-end-2024" />, while OSAM-1, a billion-dollar-class program with the field's best review culture, was cancelled before it flew <Cite id="osam1-discontinued-2024" />. The reliability-gap module's compounding arithmetic applies to a rover that must survive thousands of sols, but the deeper lesson for learned policies is evidentiary: flight heritage is the only currency this field accepts, and heritage is accumulated one bounded, supervised increment at a time, of which AEGIS's classifier inside a verified rover is the flight-proven example <Cite id="aegis-curiosity-2017" />.

Third, a calibration for claims. When a manipulation system is described as operating in unstructured environments, the honest comparator includes systems that operate where the environment was never mapped, the supervision never arrives in time, and the warranty is one-way. The Mars rovers and the commercial servicers hold that bar with classical, verified autonomy and a decade of qualification between design and flight. A learned policy will eventually hold it too, and the path there runs through exactly the niches AEGIS occupies: bounded decisions, inside verified systems, where the value of deciding onboard is measurable in watts and bits <Cite id="perseverance-autonomy-2023" />. Between here and a learned system on Mars, most of the remaining distance is the part of engineering that proves, before launch, what the system does in the case it was never shown.
